On nights with alcohol, HRV averages 88.3 ms vs 127.6 ms sober — a difference of 39.3 ms (Cohen's d = -1.47, n=119 vs 386).
Sober nights: HRV averages 127.6 ms (n=386) — her baseline before any other factor moves.
The cost is one night, not a weekend: recovery drops to 46.8% the morning after (only 8.4% of those mornings hit 80+), then is back near baseline by the next morning (68.1%, 39.8% at 80+).
7 of her 210 best-HRV days followed a drink, versus 78 of her 209 worst-HRV days.

80+ recovery isn't a baseline she returns to — it happens on 43.8% of sober days and 36.4% of all days. Reaching it after a drink takes a median of 2 days simply because that's how many rolls of the die it takes on a good week (23.1% never get there within 5 days).
This model explains 26% of day-to-day HRV variance (R²=0.258, n=775). The rest is unmeasured — stress, illness, travel, things this export doesn't capture.
REM sleep has no detectable relationship with her HRV (r=-0.052, p=0.14) — despite what sleep-tracker marketing implies.

signal_panel.label: Resting heart rate
signal_panel.text: r = -0.888 with HRV (n=799) — the strongest number in this whole dataset, and the least useful. RHR and HRV are two readings of the same autonomic state, taken in the same sleep window. A slider here would say 'lower your resting heart rate to raise your HRV' — circular, not actionable.

values.label: Resting heart rate
values.why: Same autonomic state as HRV, same measurement window — putting this in the app would say 'lower your RHR to raise your HRV', which is circular.

signal_panel.label: Respiratory rate
signal_panel.text: r = -0.337 with HRV (n=799). Strong predictor, but not something you decide to change — it stays in the fitted model as a covariate, held at her median of 15.9 rpm, because removing it inflates the alcohol coefficient (see model variants: -32.25 vs -27.72 ms).
